references.label: China’s balance of payments trade surplus diverges from China’s customs trade surplus
see Anna Wong’s paper for the Federal Reserve Board

metadata_extension.subtitle: China has a new way of calculating its good surplus in its formal balance of payments data. It is a deeply misleading. It also explains the apparent fall in the current account account surplus.

summary.central_question: Why does China's balance of payments goods surplus diverge so sharply from its customs goods surplus, and what does that mean for assessing China's current account?
summary.main_thesis: The fall in China's reported current account surplus since 2021 is mainly an artifact of an unjustified methodology change; China's true surplus is far larger, as the customs data shows.

content.text: Why does China's balance of payments goods surplus diverge so sharply from its customs goods surplus, and what does that mean for assessing China's current account?
content.reason: When two official measures of the same quantity diverge sharply, the cause of the gap must be explained before either is used.

passages.source_excerpt: It at least explains why China’s balance of payments trade surplus diverges from China’s customs trade surplus, and why the gap started to explode around 2022.

content.text: The balance of payments exists to track foreign exchange flows, so transactions that never move foreign exchange should not change the true external balance.
content.reason: External accounts should record only transactions that affect a country's foreign exchange position.

passages.source_excerpt: Production in China for sale in China has no impact on the flow of foreign exchange and thus the “true” balance of payments.

content.text: A reclassification that shifts profit offshore should be offset by changes in the income and services lines, leaving the overall balance unchanged.
content.reason: A pure change in classification moves amounts between accounts without changing the total.

passages.source_excerpt: In other words, there should be offsetting adjustments in other parts of the balance of payments—the aggregate balance should not change.

content.text: Customs data, which records goods physically crossing the border, measures China's real trade better than survey-based balance of payments data.
content.reason: Directly observed physical flows are a firmer guide than model-based or survey-based estimates.

passages.source_excerpt: And my strong view is that the customs data—which captures actual trade—gets the story right, not the marked to model (and internal survey) current account data.

content.text: China's pre-2020 methodology (customs imports minus about 5 percent for insurance and freight) remains a valid baseline for what the balance of payments goods data should show.
content.reason: A long-standing stable relationship between two series is a fair counterfactual for judging a break in that relationship.

content.text: The large-enterprise survey does not capture real cross-border activity that customs data misses, so the gap reflects measurement error rather than genuine economic flows.
content.reason: An unverifiable data source that departs from verifiable data should be presumed wrong unless shown otherwise.

content.text: Under factoryless manufacturing, a contract manufacturer's delivery to a foreign firm inside China is recorded as an export, and the foreign firm's sale back into China as an import; the markup turns into a goods deficit.
content.reason: Recording transactions by residency rather than border crossing can create trade in goods that never leave the country.

passages.source_excerpt: Such goods are now being counted as an import in the balance of payments data.

content.text: The IMF staff report's Appendix VII confirms that factoryless manufacturing transactions have been reducing China's BOP goods surplus.
content.reason: An international institution's description of an official methodology is authoritative evidence of how that methodology works.

passages.source_excerpt: When a Chinese contractor sells produced goods to the nonresident enterprise that outsourced the production, exports of goods are recorded in BOP even if the goods remain in China

content.text: A trade deficit arising from domestic production for the domestic market is economically meaningless.
content.reason: A measured external flow with no counterpart in cross-border activity is an accounting artifact.

passages.source_excerpt: So Chinese production for the Chinese market by foreign firms is somehow generating a trade deficit in the balance of payments data. This, of course, makes no real economic sense.

content.text: The goods divergence is not offset elsewhere in the current account; the gap between the customs and current account figures is even larger than the goods gap.
content.reason: If a reclassification changes the aggregate balance, it is not merely a reclassification.

passages.source_excerpt: Rather, the gap between the reported current account surplus and the customs goods data (and the customs goods data adjusted for the tourism/travel deficit) is even bigger than the custom goods to balance of payments goods gap.

content.text: BOP exports fall well below customs exports, while BOP imports exceed customs imports despite the freight adjustment that should keep them lower; this is consistent with Adam Wolf's work.
content.reason: Divergences on both sides of the ledger that run against the expected adjustment signal a measurement break.

passages.source_excerpt: Balance of payments exports are way below customs exports, and balance of payments imports are now higher than customs imports when they should be lower

content.text: Foreign firms have tax incentives to shift profits out of China, so huge in-China markups by foreign firms are implausible.
content.reason: Multinationals price transfers so as to book profits in low-tax jurisdictions without capital controls.

passages.source_excerpt: China is not a low jurisdiction, so firms generally do not want to show large Chinese profits.

content.text: Since 2022 the BOP goods data has come from direct reporting by about 13,000 large enterprises plus bank payment records, so no one can replicate it from customs data.
content.reason: Data that cannot be independently replicated deserves less trust.

passages.source_excerpt: the data is all coming from an impossible to verify internal survey and not from an adjustment to the customs data.

content.text: China has a history of opportune methodology changes, such as the 2015 tourism spending revision documented by Anna Wong, that reduced its reported surplus.
content.reason: A source with a record of convenient revisions merits scepticism toward new ones.

passages.source_excerpt: That ancient sage just highlights how China has a history of changing the methodology it uses to calculate the components of the current account at opportune times.

content.text: The BOP goods surplus is about $300 billion (over 1.5% of GDP) too small, and the Q2 current account was about $150 billion below what it should have been.
content.reason: The size of a measurement gap determines whether it matters for macro assessment.

content.text: Correcting the goods data, the author estimates China's current account surplus at close to $700 billion.
content.reason: Replace a flawed official series with one built on the pre-break methodology.

passages.source_excerpt: I personally now estimate the current account surplus to be close to $700 billion even after the drop tied the resumption of tourism in 2023.

content.text: The fall in China's reported current account surplus since 2021 is mainly an artifact of an unjustified methodology change; China's true surplus is far larger, as the customs data shows.
content.reason: When an official balance shifts only because of methodology, the underlying physical data reveal the real position.

passages.source_excerpt: the fall in China’s surplus since 2021 is basically an artifact of difficult-to-justify changes in China’s balance of payments methodology. The real story is found in the old fashioned goods data.

content.text: The IMF and other global monitors should stop relying on China's reported current account surplus in their assessments.
content.reason: Surveillance bodies should not base assessments on data known to be distorted.

passages.source_excerpt: the IMF and other guardians of the global economy absolutely should stop using China’s reported current account surplus

content.text: Many analysts take China's reported current account decline at face value as evidence of a shrinking impact on the world.
content.reason: Headline official aggregates can mislead users who do not examine methodology.

passages.source_excerpt: a large number of analysts are using China’s current account data to assess China’s impact on the world without realizing

content.text: Recording contract-manufactured goods as exports is legitimate when they are actually shipped abroad; only the in-China resale case is problematic.
content.reason: A methodology may be valid in some cases even if it distorts others.
